title: Client–Server & HTTP
subtitle: How your app talks to a server — and why it scales
objectives: Explain the request/response model and what's inside an HTTP request
Choose the right HTTP method and reason about safe retries with idempotency
Read status codes as signals about where a system is failing
Explain why stateless HTTP is what lets a service scale to thousands of servers

exercises.prompt: You open a social app and your feed appears. Where did that data physically come from the instant you opened it?
choices: It was already fully stored on your phone
Your phone asked a server, and the server answered
Another user's phone sent it straight to you
exercises.why: This is the client–server model: your phone (the client) sends a request, and a server sends back a response. Your phone stores almost none of the data — it just knows how to ask.
exercises.goDeeper: One server answers millions of clients. That asymmetry — few servers, many clients — is the shape of almost every system you'll design.

exercises.prompt: The machine that asks is the ______; the machine that answers is the server.
exercises.why: Client = asks, server = answers. They're roles, not fixed machines.
exercises.goDeeper: A 'server' can itself be a 'client' of another server — your API server calling Stripe's payments API is a client in that conversation. The roles nest.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of an HTTP request to its job.

pairs.right: What you want to do (GET, POST)

exercises.why: Every request is: a method (the verb), a path (the noun), headers (context), and an optional body (the payload).
exercises.goDeeper: A GET usually has no body — it just names what it wants. A POST carries its data in the body. HTTP is plain text under the hood; you could type a request by hand.

exercises.prompt: Order one request/response round trip.
steps: Client sends it to the server
exercises.why: Ask, travel, process, answer, render — the loop behind every screen you've ever loaded.
exercises.goDeeper: The 'travel' step includes the network round-trips you met in Unit 1. On HTTPS, a TLS handshake happens first to encrypt everything.

exercises.prompt: You send one request, then another. By default, does the server remember your first request when handling the second?
choices: No — each HTTP request is independent (stateless)
Only if both are GET requests
Only if they're within one second
exercises.why: HTTP is stateless: by default each request stands entirely on its own. The server doesn't inherently remember the last one.
exercises.goDeeper: So how does 'staying logged in' work? The client re-sends proof — a cookie or token — on every single request. State lives with the client or in a shared store, NOT in one server's memory. Hold onto this: it's the secret to scaling, and the boss lesson of this unit.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best captures what HTTP is?
choices: A database that stores your data
A stateless request/response protocol for clients and servers to talk
exercises.why: HTTP is the agreed language of the web: a stateless protocol where clients make requests and servers return responses.

exercises.prompt: You want to fetch a user's profile without changing anything. Which method?
exercises.why: GET reads data and shouldn't change anything on the server. It's the default 'just show me' verb.
exercises.goDeeper: GET is 'safe' — search-engine crawlers and browser prefetchers fire GETs freely. So never hide a state-changing action (like /delete?id=42) behind a GET, or a crawler could wipe your data just by following links. This has actually happened to real companies.

exercises.prompt: Match each method to its intent.
exercises.why: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, DELETE removes. The method tells the server your intent.
exercises.goDeeper: PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH updates just part of it. Choosing precisely is what makes an API predictable.

exercises.prompt: Which of these methods are expected to change state on the server? Select all.
exercises.why: POST, PUT, and DELETE modify server state. GET (and HEAD, OPTIONS) are 'safe' — they only read.
exercises.goDeeper: Because GET is safe, it's cacheable and retryable with zero risk. That single property is why the web can cache so aggressively.

exercises.prompt: Your DELETE /users/42 request times out and you don't know if it worked. Is it safe to just send it again?
choices: Yes — deleting twice leaves the same result as deleting once
No — you might delete two different users
No — DELETE can never be retried
Only if you switch to GET first
exercises.why: DELETE is idempotent: DELETE /users/42 twice still leaves user 42 gone. Same end state, so retrying is safe.
exercises.goDeeper: Idempotent = doing it again lands you in the same state. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not. This is the backbone of reliable distributed systems, because networks fail mid-request constantly and retries are unavoidable.

exercises.prompt: A POST /payments request times out. You don't know if the charge went through. Retrying blindly risks charging the customer twice. What's the fix?
choices: Send an idempotency key so the server recognizes the retry and doesn't repeat the charge
Change it to a GET request
exercises.why: An idempotency key is a unique id the client attaches to the request. If the server sees the same key twice, it returns the original result instead of charging again — making an unsafe POST safe to retry.
exercises.goDeeper: This is exactly how Stripe works: you send an 'Idempotency-Key' header, and Stripe dedupes retries. Any system with money or side effects needs this pattern.

exercises.prompt: An operation is ______ if performing it many times has the same effect as performing it once.
exercises.why: Idempotent operations are safe to retry — critical, because in a distributed system retries are not optional.

exercises.prompt: A server replies with 200. At a glance, what does that number tell you?
exercises.why: Status codes are the server's one-glance verdict on your request. 200 = OK, it worked.
exercises.goDeeper: The first digit is everything: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx you (the client) messed up, 5xx I (the server) messed up. Learn the classes and you can read any code you've never seen.

exercises.prompt: Match each status code to its meaning.
exercises.why: One code from each class: 2xx worked, 3xx go elsewhere, 4xx your request was wrong, 5xx the server failed.
exercises.goDeeper: Two you'll use constantly: 201 Created (a POST made something new) and 204 No Content (success, but nothing to return — perfect for a DELETE).

exercises.prompt: Which of these are CLIENT errors (the caller's fault)? Select all.
exercises.why: 4xx codes blame the request; 5xx codes blame the server. 503 is a server-side 'I can't handle this right now.'
exercises.goDeeper: Don't confuse 401 and 403. 401 Unauthorized really means 'I don't know who you are' (not authenticated). 403 Forbidden means 'I know who you are, and you're not allowed' (authenticated but no permission).

exercises.prompt: Your service is getting hammered with more traffic than it can handle. Which status code politely tells clients to slow down?
exercises.why: 429 Too Many Requests is the rate-limiting signal. Well-behaved clients back off when they see it, often honoring a 'Retry-After' header the server sends.
exercises.goDeeper: Pair 429 with exponential backoff on the client (wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s...). Without backoff, clients retry instantly in unison and create a 'thundering herd' that keeps the service down.

exercises.prompt: Your app sits behind a load balancer. Users start seeing 502 and 504 errors. Where is the problem most likely?
choices: Downstream of the load balancer — the app servers are failing or too slow
exercises.why: 502 Bad Gateway means the load balancer got a broken response from the app behind it; 504 Gateway Timeout means the app didn't respond in time. Both point downstream — the app or database, not the balancer or the client.
exercises.goDeeper: This is why status codes are gold during an incident: 502/504 → look at the app tier; 503 → the service is shedding load; 500 → an unhandled crash in your code. The code tells you which layer to open first.

exercises.prompt: A user requests GET /orders/99999, but no such order exists. What should the server return?
exercises.why: The resource genuinely doesn't exist and the client's request was well-formed — that's a textbook 404. Returning 200 for a missing resource lies to the client and breaks caching and error handling.
exercises.goDeeper: Returning the honest code matters: monitoring, retries, and caches all make decisions based on it. A 500 here would page an engineer for a non-bug; a 200 would hide a real 'not found.'

exercises.prompt: A big service runs thousands of identical web servers behind one load balancer, and each of your requests may hit a different server — yet everything works. Why is that possible?
choices: The servers share one block of memory
HTTP is stateless, so any server can handle any request
Your requests secretly always hit the same server
The load balancer copies your data to every server
exercises.why: Because each request carries everything needed to serve it (like an auth token), any interchangeable server can handle any request. Statelessness is what makes horizontal scaling possible.
exercises.goDeeper: The moment a server stores your session in its own local memory, servers stop being interchangeable — now the load balancer must pin you to that one machine ('sticky sessions'), and if it dies, your session dies with it.

exercises.prompt: If servers remember nothing between requests, where does your logged-in session actually live?
choices: In the client (a cookie/token it re-sends), or in a shared store like Redis
exercises.why: State moves out of the server: either the client carries it (a token sent on every request) or it lives in a shared store all servers can read. Never in one server's local RAM.
exercises.goDeeper: Two common patterns: a self-contained token (JWT) the client carries, or a session id the client carries that servers look up in a shared cache (Redis). Both keep the servers stateless and interchangeable.

exercises.prompt: Place the missing piece so any app server can serve any request without losing the user's session.
exercises.why: A shared store that every app server reads from keeps sessions out of local memory, so the servers stay stateless and interchangeable.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the standard fix for 'randomly logged out' bugs: move session state to a shared cache, and it no longer matters which server you land on.

exercises.prompt: Opening a fresh TCP + TLS connection for every single request is expensive. Which of these reduce that cost? Select all.
choices: Keep-alive: reuse one connection for many requests
HTTP/2 multiplexing: many requests in flight on one connection
Opening a brand-new connection for every image
HTTP/3 over QUIC: avoids TCP-level head-of-line blocking
exercises.why: Reusing connections (keep-alive) and multiplexing (HTTP/2, HTTP/3) amortize the handshake cost across many requests. Opening a fresh connection each time is the problem, not a fix.
exercises.goDeeper: HTTP/1.1 could only handle one request at a time per connection — a slow response blocked everything behind it (head-of-line blocking). HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP to fix blocking that still happened at the TCP layer.

exercises.prompt: Your API serves a user avatar that rarely changes. How do you avoid re-sending the same bytes on every request?
choices: You can't — you must resend it each time
Use Cache-Control + an ETag: the client asks 'still current?' and the server can reply 304 Not Modified with no body
Make the image smaller each time
exercises.why: With an ETag (a fingerprint of the content), the client sends 'I have version X — changed?' and the server can answer 304 Not Modified with an empty body. Same-bytes are never re-sent.
exercises.goDeeper: 304 responses are a huge part of why repeat page loads feel instant — the browser revalidates cheaply and skips the download entirely.

exercises.prompt: Auth for a high-security banking app. Self-contained JWTs let any server validate locally (great for scale) but are hard to revoke before they expire. Redis-backed sessions are instantly revocable but every request hits the store. Slide toward your default here.
exercises.why: For high-security, instant revocation usually wins — if a token is stolen, you must be able to kill it NOW. A central session store gives you that, at the cost of a lookup per request. JWTs trade that away for statelessness.
exercises.goDeeper: Many real systems combine both: short-lived JWTs (minutes) plus a revocation check, getting most of JWT's scale while limiting how long a stolen token stays valid.

exercises.prompt: Users randomly get logged out, but only during high traffic. The setup: app servers store sessions in their own local memory, behind a round-robin load balancer. What's happening, and what's the fix?
choices: DNS is misconfigured — flush the cache
Round-robin sends you to servers that don't have your in-memory session → move sessions to a shared store so servers are stateless
The database ran out of disk — add storage
The users' tokens expired — shorten the timeout
exercises.why: Under load the balancer spreads you across many servers; whenever you land on one that doesn't hold your in-memory session, you appear logged out. Making the servers stateless — sessions in a shared store — fixes it permanently.
exercises.goDeeper: The band-aid is 'sticky sessions' (pin each user to one server), but that undermines load balancing and fails when a server dies. Stateless servers + a shared session store is the scalable cure — and it ties this whole unit together: stateless HTTP is what lets systems grow.
